findings.requirement_type: Professional Liability / E&O — No Policy Available for Audit
findings.contract_quote: Sacramento: 'PROFESSIONAL LIABILITY OR ERRORS AND OMISSIONS LIABILITY: $1,000,000 per claim and aggregate.' Section II.E expressly excludes umbrella from satisfying this minimum: 'Umbrella ... shall provide liability coverages that at least follow form over the underlying insurance requirements ... (other than Professional Liability).'
findings.policy_quote: No Professional Liability / E&O policy was provided for audit.
findings.policy_page: N/A — policy not in audit set
findings.gap_description: Sacramento County independently requires Professional Liability with a $1M/$1M minimum and expressly forbids using Umbrella to satisfy it. Run-Test provides election services — ballot printing accuracy, mail processing, election technology, voter data handling — these are quintessential professional services where a misprint, mis-sort, or system failure could cause significant economic loss to a county client and trigger a wrongful-act claim that GL would not cover (no bodily injury, no property damage). Without an E&O policy, every economic-damage claim from a county is uninsured. For an election-services company, this is the single most claim-likely line.
findings.plain_english: Election services is fundamentally a professional services business — accuracy of ballots, integrity of mail processing, reliability of election technology. A misprinted ballot, a mis-sorted mailing, or a software glitch could cost a county tens of millions and trigger a lawsuit. General Liability does NOT cover that — it covers bodily injury and property damage, not economic loss from a service failure. E&O / Professional Liability is the policy that responds. If you don't have it, you are uninsured for the most likely lawsuit your business will face. Sacramento expressly forbids using your umbrella to plug this hole.
findings.recommendation: Bind Technology / Miscellaneous Professional E&O immediately with a definition of 'Professional Services' that explicitly captures election technology, ballot printing/mailing, election mail processing, voter registration data services, and tabulation support. $1M/$1M minimum to satisfy Sacramento, but $5M+ should be considered given the scale ($5M-$25M revenue, 90M registered voters served). Verify retro date precedes the Sacramento contract effective date and any prior county contract dates. Negotiate consent-to-settle (hammer clause) with broker-friendly mechanics.
discoveryQuestions: If a county claimed your team mis-printed 50,000 ballots and they had to re-print and re-mail before election day, who pays for that — you, your insurer, or someone else?
Have you ever had a county or jurisdiction express concern about an error in ballot data, mailing accuracy, or technology performance? What happened?
Walk me through your professional liability policy — who's the carrier, what's the retro date, and how does the policy define 'professional services'?
When Sacramento County reviewed your insurance, were they satisfied with your E&O independently of your umbrella, since the contract specifically excludes umbrella from satisfying the E&O minimum?

The policy shall include, but not be limited to; coverage for all directors, officers, agents and employees of the Contractor, losses with respect to network risks (such as data breaches, unauthorized access or use, and ID theft of data), invasion of privacy ... crisis management, identity theft response costs, breach notification costs, credit remediation, and credit monitoring, defense, and claims expenses, regulatory defense costs plus fines and penalties, cyber extortion, electronic data restoration expenses, network business interruption, computer fraud coverage, funds transfer loss, third-party fidelity, theft, no requirement for arrest and conviction, and loss outside the premises of the named insured.'

findings.gap_description: Maricopa County mandates a $5M cyber policy with one of the broadest cyber specs we see — explicitly required components include regulatory FINES AND PENALTIES (not just defense), third-party fidelity, computer fraud, funds transfer fraud, business interruption, dependent BI, cyber extortion, breach response, credit monitoring, and crisis management, with specific carve-backs (no arrest-and-conviction requirement, off-premises losses included). Run-Test handles voter registration data, ballot delivery information, and election technology serving 90M registered voters across 31 states — this is among the highest-profile cyber/privacy risk profiles in the country given election-integrity threats and state attorney-general scrutiny. Without a cyber policy, any ransomware event, data breach, social engineering loss, or network failure is uninsured.
findings.plain_english: You handle voter data for 90 million registered Americans across 31 states. You serve county elections offices that are top-tier cyberattack targets — election infrastructure is on every nation-state actor's wish list. Maricopa demands a $5M cyber policy with one of the most comprehensive feature lists we see in any contract. Without cyber, a single ransomware event would cost Run-Test millions in forensics, restoration, breach notification, regulatory defense, business interruption, and downstream liability — all uninsured. The Maricopa requirement alone is a compliance imperative; the underlying business risk is existential.
findings.recommendation: Bind a standalone Cyber Liability policy immediately with $5M minimum limit (both per-occurrence and aggregate), affirmative grants for: (1) regulatory fines and penalties to maximum allowed by law in every state, (2) third-party fidelity / social engineering with sublimit at or near full policy limit, (3) computer fraud / funds transfer fraud, (4) business interruption with 8-12 hour waiting period, (5) dependent business interruption, (6) cyber extortion / ransomware (verify no co-insurance), (7) breach response / forensics / notification, (8) credit monitoring, (9) crisis management. Verify retro date precedes Maricopa contract effective date (per §8.2.3, two-year ERP). Coalition, Beazley, At-Bay, or AIG are appropriate markets given operations scale. Carrier rating must satisfy Maricopa B++ minimum.
discoveryQuestions: If your systems were ransomware-encrypted three weeks before a major election, what's the response plan and who pays for the forensics, recovery, and lost productivity?
Has a county risk manager or state secretary of state's office ever asked specific questions about your cybersecurity posture or breach response?
How much voter PII does Run-Test currently process — names, addresses, signatures, registration data — and where is it stored?
If a state attorney general opened an investigation tomorrow over a privacy incident at a county you serve, who would defend that — your lawyers, or an insurer's panel?

findings.contract_quote: Sacramento §II.E: 'UMBRELLA or Excess Liability policies are acceptable where the need for higher liability limits is noted ... and shall provide liability coverages that at least follow form over the underlying insurance requirements where necessary for Commercial General Liability, Commercial Automobile Liability, Employers' Liability, and any other liability coverage (other than Professional Liability) designated under the Minimum Scope of Insurance.' Maricopa §8.2.9: 'The insurance policies required by this contract may be combined with Commercial Umbrella Insurance policies to meet the minimum limit requirements.'

findings.policy_quote: No Umbrella / Excess Liability policy was provided for audit.
findings.policy_page: N/A — policy not in audit set
findings.gap_description: While neither contract independently mandates an umbrella, both contemplate one as the mechanism to reach high-limit requirements (Maricopa $2M Auto + $5M Cyber). For a $5M-$25M revenue PE-backed elections company serving 90M voters across 31 states, lack of umbrella is a critical capital structure risk — a single multi-vehicle auto accident or a class-action privacy claim could exceed primary limits. Maricopa's GL primary requirement is already $2M/$4M/$4M, which most companies layer with $5M-$25M umbrella. Without umbrella, every dollar above primary limits is uninsured exposure to balance sheet — and the indemnity-uncapped clause (Maricopa §8.1.3) means contractual liability above limits flows directly to Run-Test.
findings.plain_english: Even if all your underlying policies are perfect, a single bad day — a multi-vehicle accident, a class-action privacy lawsuit, an injury at a county facility — can blow through primary limits in hours. Umbrella is the safety net that catches that. Both counties expect you to have one, and Maricopa's contract specifically allows umbrella to stack on most lines to meet limit requirements. Without it, you're essentially betting the company on the assumption that no claim will ever exceed your underlying limits. That's not a bet a PE-backed business should be taking.
findings.recommendation: Bind a Commercial Umbrella with $10M-$25M limit minimum given operations scale. Verify follow-form for GL, Auto, Employers Liability — and explicitly confirm the umbrella DOES drop down for action-over claims, follows the underlying additional insured, primary/non-contributory, and waiver-of-subrogation status. Verify Per-Project / Per-Location aggregate follows form. Defense should be outside limits where possible. Schedule of underlying must list ALL primary policies. Confirm carrier meets Sacramento A-VII / Maricopa B++ minimums.
discoveryQuestions: What's the largest loss your business could survive without insurance — and what's your current catastrophic-claim ceiling across all lines?
Your PE sponsor likely has expectations on tower limits — has anyone modeled what would happen to enterprise value if a claim exceeded your primary policies?
If a class-action privacy lawsuit named Run-Test as a co-defendant alongside a county, do you know what your total available limits would be?
When Maricopa accepted your insurance, did you stack umbrella to meet the $2M Auto and $5M Cyber requirements, or were those satisfied by primary alone?

findings.requirement_type: WC Designated Entity NOC — Maricopa County Not Listed
findings.contract_quote: Maricopa §8.2.15: 'Applicable to all insurance policies required within the insurance requirements of this contract, Contractor's insurance shall not be permitted to expire, be suspended, be canceled, or be materially changed for any reason without 30 days prior written notice to Maricopa County.'
findings.policy_quote: Form 331-0342 (09 11) — Notice of Cancellation to Designated Entity(s). Schedule of designated entities: 'El Paso County Contracts & Procurement Division (200 South Cascade Avenue, Colorado Springs, CO 80903); Coconino County (219 East Cherry Ave, Flagstaff, AZ 86001); Amazon.com Services LLC (345 Boren Avenue North, Seattle, WA 98109).' Maricopa County is NOT listed.
findings.gap_description: The Hanover WC policy includes a designated-entity NOC mechanism (form 331-0342) that gives 30-day cancellation notice to scheduled entities. Maricopa County is conspicuously missing from the schedule — which lists Coconino County (a different AZ county), El Paso County (CO), and Amazon. The contract requires Maricopa receive 30-day notice of any cancellation, suspension, OR material change. Without Maricopa on the NOC schedule, the only mechanism for Maricopa to receive notice is the contractor's 2-business-day relay obligation under §8.2.15 — meaning Run-Test bears the full administrative burden and the consequences of any failure (which is a material breach per §8.2.2).
findings.plain_english: Your WC policy has a special endorsement that automatically tells specific government agencies if your insurance is being cancelled. Coconino County and El Paso County are on the list — but Maricopa County, the actual contract counterparty here, is NOT. That means if Hanover ever cancels or non-renews, Maricopa won't be notified by the carrier — only by you, manually, within 2 business days. If you miss that 2-day window, you're in material breach of the contract. The same form already covers Coconino and El Paso; adding Maricopa is a 5-minute fix that closes a real exposure.
findings.recommendation: Submit endorsement request to Hanover to add 'Maricopa County, c/o Risk Management, 301 W Jefferson St, Suite 910, Phoenix, AZ 85003' to the form 331-0342 schedule. Note: standard NOC endorsements typically cover cancellation/non-renewal but not 'material change' — verify the endorsement language and consider whether a custom endorsement is needed to satisfy Maricopa's broader 'material change' notice trigger. Also add Maricopa to all OTHER policies in the program once they are produced for audit (GL, Auto, Cyber, Umbrella).
discoveryQuestions: Do you know which counties are currently scheduled on your insurance cancellation-notice endorsements? Has anyone audited that list against your active contracts?
If your carrier non-renewed mid-contract, what's the operational process for notifying Maricopa within the 2-business-day window?
How many other county or government contracts do you hold where the contract requires 30-day carrier notice? Are all of them listed on the same endorsement?
Has any government client ever rejected your COI because the cancellation-notice provision wasn't on a designated-entity endorsement and was just stated on the certificate?

findings.requirement_type: Cancellation Notice Period vs. 90-Day Broker Benchmark
findings.contract_quote: Sacramento §VI.A.2 (10-day renewal evidence + immediate carrier-communication relay) and Maricopa §8.2.15 (30-day notice to County). Beyond contract minimums, Strategic Risk benchmark is 90-day notice for designated entities.
findings.contract_file: Sacramento County and Maricopa County contract requirements
findings.policy_quote: Form 331-0342: '30 days written notice to designated entities for cancellation other than nonpayment.' AZ amendatory (WC 02 06 01 C): 30-day notice to insured and Industrial Commission of Arizona.
findings.gap_description: Both contracts are satisfied at 30-day notice. However, the broker benchmark for designated-entity NOC is 90 days, providing time to remarket and bind replacement coverage without lapse. At 30 days, Run-Test may have insufficient lead time to replace coverage and remain in compliance with all government contracts simultaneously. This is a program-design observation rather than a contract violation.
findings.plain_english: Your policy meets the contract minimum (30 days) but falls short of the Strategic Risk best-practice standard of 90-day notice to government clients. Why does this matter? If a carrier non-renews in May for a July expiration, 30 days isn't enough time to remarket and bind replacement coverage cleanly — especially with multiple counties to keep informed. 90 days gives you a real working window. This is a quality-of-program issue, not a compliance failure.
findings.recommendation: At renewal, request Hanover endorse 90-day designated-entity notice on the WC, and replicate the 90-day standard across the GL, Auto, Cyber, and Umbrella once those policies are confirmed. Many standard markets will accommodate 60- or 90-day notice on request without premium impact.
discoveryQuestions: If your carrier non-renewed your WC tomorrow, how many days do you actually need to remarket and bind a replacement without a coverage lapse?
Have any of your county clients indicated they want longer notice than 30 days, or expressed concern about how late they'd find out about a coverage change?
Does your PE sponsor have any insurance covenant requiring specific notice periods that might exceed what counties demand?

findings.requirement_type: WC All States Endorsement — Item 3.A vs 3.C Coverage
findings.contract_quote: RMF WC-3: 'All States Endorsement on WC / Additionally are any states omitted from 3.A that were picked up under 3.C in the previous year? If so, this can be very problematic.'
findings.policy_quote: Item 3.A states: AZ, AR, CA, CO, FL, GA, IL, IN, MN, NY, NC, OR, PA, SD. Item 3.C: 'All states except ND, OH, WA, WY (monopolistic) and the states named in 3.A.' Run-Test serves clients in 31 states + DC.
findings.gap_description: 14 states are scheduled in Item 3.A as primary covered states with full statutory coverage from day one. Item 3.C Other States Insurance covers all non-monopolistic remaining states. The Workers Compensation Broad Form Endorsement (990301B0316) extends Other States Insurance protection to a 60-day notification window for new states (vs 30 days standard). Stop Gap Coverage is provided for the four monopolistic states (ND/OH/WA/WY) — except in Indiana where the Broad Form is fully deleted. With Run-Test serving 31 states + DC, this construction is appropriately broad.
findings.plain_english: Workers' comp coverage rules differ by state, and a policy that doesn't list every state where you have employees can leave gaps. Your WC policy lists 14 'primary' states plus an 'all other states' clause covering everywhere except the four monopolistic states (where state-fund coverage is required and your policy provides Stop Gap protection). Combined with the Broad Form Endorsement, this gives you 60-day coverage in any new state you enter. Well-constructed for a 31-state operation.
findings.recommendation: Run a payroll-by-state report at each renewal and confirm any state with material payroll is in 3.A (not just 3.C). 3.A is preferred because rates are pre-filed and audited; 3.C can result in audit-time surprises. findings.requirement_type: Alternate Employer Endorsement / Staffing Arrangement
findings.contract_quote: RMF WC-5: 'Alternate Employee Endorsement included on the leasing company's policy?'

findings.plain_english: Election cycles create big seasonal staffing surges. If Run-Test brings in temps from a staffing company during peak periods, you need to be sure the staffing company's workers' comp covers them when they're at your facility — and that includes an 'alternate employer endorsement' naming you as a co-employer. If it doesn't, an injured temp can sue Run-Test directly in tort court (where damages are uncapped), bypassing the workers' comp 'exclusive remedy' shield that protects you from your own employees' lawsuits. This is one of the biggest hidden exposures in seasonal manufacturing.
findings.recommendation: Confirm whether Run-Test uses temporary or leased labor. If yes: (1) collect WC certificates from each staffing vendor showing Run-Test as alternate employer, (2) require the WC 00 03 01 A Alternate Employer endorsement on each staffing firm's policy, (3) verify the staffing firm has the right state coverage for any state Run-Test deploys to. Consider adding the Alternate Employer endorsement to Run-Test's own WC if Run-Test ever loans employees to other entities.

findings.requirement_type: Small Indemnity Claims & Back-to-Work Program
findings.contract_quote: RMF WC-1: '# & amount of small indemnity claims in experience period - Can these be treated, in the future, with the utilization of a 'back to work' program, as medical only claims. Will this result in a 70% reduction for mod calculation purposes for those NCCI states that allow such an adjustment?'
findings.policy_quote: Loss runs and individual claim detail not provided in the policy summary.
findings.gap_description: NCCI rules (in most states) reduce the experience-mod impact of small indemnity claims by 70% if they can be reclassified as medical-only via an effective return-to-work / modified-duty program. Run-Test's mod is already favorable (0.69 in most states), but a single small indemnity claim avoiding RTW could swing the mod and cost real premium. Without loss run review, RTW program effectiveness can't be assessed.
findings.plain_english: Small workers' comp claims that involve any time-off-work get 'indemnity' status, which hurts your experience mod 3x harder than the same claim treated as 'medical only.' A real return-to-work / modified-duty program — where injured workers come back on light duty fast — converts indemnity claims into medical-only and saves you mod points. Your mod is already strong, but a back-to-work program is how you keep it that way.
findings.recommendation: Request Hanover loss runs covering the most recent 5 years. Identify any indemnity claims under $10K and assess whether RTW could have prevented or shortened time-off. Establish or formalize a written modified-duty program if one doesn't exist. Track success metrics annually.

In states without the 70% indemnity reduction, paying very small claims out-of-pocket (rather than through the carrier) can keep them off the mod entirely. This is most effective for sub-$1K medical-only claims.
findings.plain_english: Some workers' comp claims are so small that running them through the carrier costs you more in mod-impact than just paying them yourself out of pocket. For example, a $400 urgent-care visit reported and paid by the carrier hurts your mod for three years; paid directly, it doesn't appear at all. We should review your loss runs to identify any candidates.
findings.recommendation: Identify any sub-$1K medical-only claims in the last 3-5 years. Discuss with broker and CFO a policy for pay-direct on de minimis claims (compliant with state law — some states require all claims be reported). Coordinate with HR on injury reporting protocols.

findings.requirement_type: Large Claims Management & Reserves Review
findings.contract_quote: RMF WC-10: 'Large claims by name and total incurred - Have these been managed correctly?'
findings.policy_quote: Loss runs not in policy summary. No large open or closed claims identified in available data.
findings.gap_description: The favorable experience mods (0.66-0.97) suggest no severe historical claims, but specific large-claim review (claims with reserves >$25K) is the standard audit step. Reserves are a major mod driver — over-reserved open claims inflate the mod even if they ultimately settle for less. Quarterly reserve review with claims adjuster is industry best practice.
findings.plain_english: When you have an open workers' comp claim, the carrier sets a 'reserve' — basically their estimate of what it'll cost. That reserve, not the actual eventual payment, drives your mod for 3 years. If the carrier over-reserves a claim that later settles small, you pay for a high mod for 3 years anyway. Quarterly reserve review with the adjuster — pushing back on inflated reserves — is how you protect the mod proactively.
findings.recommendation: Establish quarterly claims review meetings with Hanover claims adjuster. Identify any open claim with reserves >$25K and challenge or validate. Track reserve movements over time. For any closed claim with significant reserve > settlement variance, request retroactive mod adjustment.

Sacramento's contract acknowledges this — your AI coverage to the County applies, but not for the County's own active negligence. This is standard contract language but it has real teeth. If a $10M judgment lands, your insurance pays its limit and the rest is on your balance sheet. findings.policy_quote: N/A — conditional requirement only triggered if Run-Test maintains COC/Builders Risk for construction work.
findings.gap_description: Run-Test does not appear to perform construction subject to COC/Builders Risk. N/A.
findings.plain_english: N/A — this only applies if you're running a construction project, which you're not.

findings.requirement_type: Inland Marine Waiver of Subrogation
findings.contract_quote: Sacramento §IX: 'Any Inland Marine insurance policies maintained by the CONTRACTOR in performance of the Agreement shall be endorsed to state that the insurer shall waive all rights of subrogation against the COUNTY.'
findings.policy_quote: N/A — Inland Marine policy not in audit set.
findings.gap_description: Run-Test profile flags 'High-value equipment' as a special risk, and elections technology routinely involves high-value equipment in transit (scanners, tabulators, ballot-on-demand printers, signature verification systems) — classic Inland Marine exposure. If an Inland Marine / Equipment Floater policy is in force, it must include a waiver of subrogation in favor of the County. Cannot verify without the IM policy.
findings.plain_english: Sacramento expects that if you have Inland Marine coverage on your equipment (which moves between locations), the carrier waives the right to come after the County if equipment is damaged on county property. Given Run-Test's high-value election equipment that moves between facilities and counties, you almost certainly have an Inland Marine policy or equipment floater. We need to confirm it's in place, includes blanket WoS, and lists the high-value equipment by category.
findings.recommendation: Produce Inland Marine / Equipment Floater policy for audit. Verify (1) blanket WoS endorsement, (2) coverage limit adequate for total equipment value, (3) transit, off-premises, and county-premises locations all covered, (4) named insureds match WC entity list (4 entities).

findings.requirement_type: Subcontractor Pass-Through Insurance Requirements
findings.contract_quote: Sacramento §VII.E: 'CONTRACTOR shall be responsible for the acts and omissions of all its subcontractors and additional insured endorsements as provided by CONTRACTOR's subcontractor.'
findings.policy_quote: N/A — sub-contract management process question.
findings.gap_description: Run-Test is responsible for subcontractor acts/omissions and must ensure subs provide AI endorsements flowing through to the County. No subcontractor management process is documented in available data. Common gaps: subs with sub-limit policies, subs not listing County as AI, subs without WC, missing pass-through indemnity/insurance language in sub-contracts.
findings.plain_english: If you use subcontractors — printers, mail vendors, IT contractors, software providers — Sacramento holds you responsible for them. You need each one to (a) carry insurance matching what the County requires of you, (b) name the County as additional insured, and (c) have a written contract with you that flows down all the same insurance terms. We need to see your subcontractor agreement template and a sample COI from a recent sub to verify.
findings.recommendation: Request: (1) standard subcontractor agreement template Run-Test uses, (2) sample COI from a recent subcontractor. Verify pass-through insurance/indemnity language matches Sacramento and Maricopa county minimums. Build a sub-COI tracking system with calendar reminders for renewal cycles.

findings.requirement_type: WC TRIPRA Terrorism Coverage

Your workers' comp properly includes federally-backed terrorism coverage so that if an act of terrorism injures employees at a Run-Test facility or election site, the carrier responds (with the federal government picking up 80% above the carrier's deductible). Solid construction.

findings.contract_quote: RMF WC-6 / Oregon-specific WC 36 03 06 EL minimum requirements.

findings.contract_quote: RMF WC-6 — NY-specific limit construction.

findings.requirement_type: Audit Noncompliance Charge — California 3X Multiplier
findings.contract_quote: Standard premium-audit best practice and CA-specific exposure.
findings.policy_quote: Form WC 04 04 21 — Optional Premium Increase Endorsement (CA): 'If audit access not provided within 90 days post-expiration, insured liable for 3X current annual premium estimate plus audit attempt costs.' Florida WC 09 04 07 A: 'up to 3X most recent estimated annual premium for audit non-cooperation; $500 cost-defrayment for denied physical inspection; 10X penalty + attorney fees for understated/concealed payroll.' WC 00 04 24 audit non-compliance charge (general): up to 2X estimated annual premium.
findings.gap_description: Severe audit-noncompliance penalties exist in CA (3X), FL (3X / 10X for concealed payroll + attorney fees), and across the program (2X). For a multi-state employer with $30K+ premium, audit noncompliance could result in $60K-$100K+ in penalty premium. Run-Test must have a robust audit response process given multi-state, multi-class operations.
findings.plain_english: If you don't cooperate with the carrier's annual premium audit, the penalties are punitive — California can charge 3 times the premium, Florida can charge 3 times normally and 10 times if they find you under-reported payroll (plus attorney fees). For a $30K+ premium, that's a $60K-$300K downside risk. Build a calendar reminder and a clean audit-prep process.
findings.recommendation: Establish annual audit response process: (1) calendar reminder 30 days before audit window, (2) pre-prepared payroll-by-state, payroll-by-class breakdown, (3) classification documentation supporting any disputed codes, (4) named audit contact. Document Florida-specific quarterly earnings reports submitted to FL DOR with sworn officer attestation per WC 09 04 07 A.

findings.requirement_type: Maricopa Cancellation 'Material Change' Notice — Broader Than Standard NOC
findings.contract_quote: Maricopa §8.2.15: 'Contractor's insurance shall not be permitted to expire, be suspended, be canceled, or be materially changed for any reason without 30 days prior written notice to Maricopa County.'
findings.policy_quote: Form 331-0342 — Notice of Cancellation to Designated Entity(s): '30 days written notice to designated entities for cancellation other than nonpayment.'
findings.gap_description: Maricopa's notice requirement covers cancellation, expiration, suspension, AND 'material change.' Standard NOC endorsement form 331-0342 covers cancellation only — not 'material change' (e.g., limit reduction, coverage carve-out, named insured deletion). Even if Maricopa were on the schedule (which it isn't — see separate finding), the endorsement wouldn't satisfy the 'material change' notice trigger. Run-Test's 2-business-day relay obligation under §8.2.15 partially fills this — but only after Run-Test learns of the change.
findings.plain_english: Maricopa wants 30-day notice not just for outright cancellations but for 'material changes' — limit drops, coverage carve-outs, or anyone deleted from the policy. Standard cancellation-notice endorsements don't cover material changes. The contract puts that burden on you (the contractor) to relay any such notice within 2 business days. The exposure is procedural: a quiet mid-term limit reduction could happen without anyone noticing until a claim hits.
findings.recommendation: Negotiate with Hanover to expand 331-0342 (or replace with a custom endorsement) to include material-change notice for designated entities. As a backup process control, schedule quarterly review of all required policies for any mid-term endorsements that constitute 'material change' and report them to Maricopa (and Sacramento) within 2 business days as required.
discoveryQuestions: If Hanover endorsed a coverage reduction mid-term, what's the workflow that would surface that to Maricopa within 2 business days?
Has Run-Test ever had a mid-term policy change that should have been reported to a county client? What happened?
Who at Run-Test owns the insurance file day-to-day and reviews carrier endorsement issuances as they arrive?

findings.requirement_type: Sacramento Right to Adjust Coverage (Open-Ended Risk)
findings.contract_quote: Sacramento §II.B (preamble): 'COUNTY shall retain the right at any time to review the coverage, form, and amount of the insurance required hereby. If in the opinion of the County Risk Manager, insurance provisions in these requirements do not provide adequate protection ... COUNTY may require CONTRACTOR to obtain insurance sufficient in coverage, form and amount to provide adequate protection.'
findings.policy_quote: N/A — open-ended contract risk, not a policy form question.
findings.gap_description: Sacramento has a unilateral right to demand additional coverage mid-term. Open-ended exposure: limits, lines, and endorsements could grow at the County's discretion. This is a contract-level concern, not a policy gap, but should be flagged for the CFO's awareness.
findings.plain_english: Sacramento reserved the right to come back later and say, 'We want more insurance from you.' They can change limits, demand new lines, or insist on new endorsements — and you have to comply. Most CFOs miss this clause. It's not a coverage gap, but it's a budget risk we should plan for.
findings.recommendation: Brief CFO and PE sponsor on this clause. Build a 10-15% contingency into the insurance budget for any contract Run-Test signs with this language. Any County demand for coverage adjustment goes through broker for negotiation before binding — Sacramento may accept alternatives.

findings.requirement_type: Maricopa Notification of Claim / Lawsuit (Sacramento parallel)
findings.contract_quote: Sacramento §X: 'CONTRACTOR shall give prompt and timely notice ... within thirty (30) days following the date of receipt of a claim or ten (10) days following the date of service of process of a lawsuit.'
findings.policy_quote: N/A — operational obligation on contractor.
findings.gap_description: Run-Test has direct contractual obligation to notify the County of any claim within 30 days of receipt and any lawsuit within 10 days of service. This is independent of carrier reporting obligations. Run-Test needs an internal claims-tracking workflow that triggers notice to the County, not just the carrier. Failure could create breach exposure beyond any insurance issue.
findings.plain_english: If anyone sues Run-Test or files a claim that could affect the County, Sacramento wants to know within 30 days (claim) or 10 days (lawsuit) — separately from telling your insurance carrier. Most companies have a process for the carrier; few have a parallel process for client notification. We need to build that.
findings.recommendation: Build internal claim/lawsuit tracking process with two-track notice obligation: (1) carrier notice per policy terms, (2) client notice per contract terms. Calendar reminders set for 30-day and 10-day clocks. Standard form letter to County drafted and reviewed by counsel. Apply same workflow to Maricopa and any other government client with similar provisions.

findings.requirement_type: Crime / Fidelity / Social Engineering — No Standalone Policy in Audit Set
findings.contract_quote: Maricopa cyber spec §8.2.13 expressly requires: 'computer fraud coverage, funds transfer loss, third-party fidelity, theft, no requirement for arrest and conviction.'
findings.policy_quote: No Crime / Fidelity / Social Engineering policy in audit set. Maricopa explicitly requires these features inside the Cyber spec.
findings.gap_description: Maricopa's cyber spec mandates components that traditionally live in a Crime/Fidelity policy: third-party fidelity, computer fraud, funds transfer loss, theft. Election services companies handle voter list payments, vendor payments, and county-flow funds — exposures to vendor impersonation, employee theft, and wire-transfer fraud are real. Even if cyber covers some of these (often sublimited), a standalone Crime policy is the proper home. PE-backed structures often discover this gap during a CFO-level treasury fraud event.
findings.plain_english: Maricopa's cyber spec mixes features that usually live in TWO different policies — the cyber stuff (data breach, ransomware) and the crime stuff (employee theft, wire fraud, social engineering). Many cyber forms include the crime components only as low sublimits (often $100K-$250K against your $5M tower). A standalone Crime policy gives full limits for theft and funds transfer. Given how exposed election services is to vendor-impersonation and wire fraud, a Crime policy belongs in the program.
findings.recommendation: Bind a standalone Crime / Commercial Crime policy with: $1M-$5M Employee Theft, $1M+ Computer Fraud, $1M+ Funds Transfer Fraud, $250K+ Social Engineering / Impersonation Fraud, Third-Party Fidelity. Treat as complement to Cyber, not substitute. Travelers, Hartford, Chubb are appropriate markets.
discoveryQuestions: What's your wire transfer authorization process — is it dual-control, and how often does it touch payments to county or vendor accounts?
Has Run-Test ever experienced a vendor-impersonation or 'CEO fraud' attempt where someone tried to redirect a payment? What happened?
If an employee in your AP department wired $250K to a fraudulent account based on a spoofed vendor email, is that covered by your current cyber policy — and if so, at what sublimit?
Has your treasury team ever evaluated a standalone Crime policy alongside Cyber, or is the assumption that Cyber covers all funds-transfer risk?

findings.requirement_type: EPLI / Employment Practices — Not in Audit Set
findings.contract_quote: WC EL exclusion §C.7 (Page 102): 'Excludes damages from coercion, criticism, demotion, evaluation, reassignment, discipline, defamation, harassment, humiliation, discrimination, termination, or any personnel practices/policies/acts/omissions. EPLI required to fill this gap.'
findings.policy_quote: WC EL excludes employment-practices claims; no EPLI policy in audit set.
findings.gap_description: Workers' comp EL expressly excludes employment-practices liability — the most common employee lawsuit category (wrongful termination, harassment, discrimination, retaliation). With 50-200 employees in a multi-state operation, statistically Run-Test will face an EPLI claim. PE-backed companies frequently have heightened EPLI risk during integration / restructuring periods. Without a standalone EPLI policy, every employment lawsuit is uninsured.
findings.plain_english: Your workers' comp will not cover the most common employee lawsuit you'll face — wrongful termination, harassment, discrimination, retaliation, hostile work environment claims. Those need a standalone Employment Practices Liability (EPLI) policy. With 50-200 employees, multi-state, PE-backed (which often correlates with integration/turnover stress), this is one of the highest-likelihood gaps in the program. We didn't see EPLI in the audit set.
findings.recommendation: Bind standalone EPLI with $1M-$3M limit minimum, third-party coverage (harassment by/against non-employees), wage & hour defense costs sublimit, broad definition of 'employee' to include temps/contractors. Travelers, Hartford, AIG, Chubb appropriate. Often packaged with D&O as Management Liability — verify packaging with broker.
discoveryQuestions: What's your turnover rate, and have you had any employee complaints, EEOC charges, or wage/hour claims in the last 3 years?
If a terminated employee sued for wrongful termination next month, who would defend that claim and pay any settlement?
Has your PE sponsor surveyed portfolio companies on EPLI specifically? Many sponsors require it as a baseline policy.
How often do supervisors get harassment / discrimination training, and is that documented?

findings.requirement_type: D&O / Management Liability — Not in Audit Set
findings.contract_quote: PE-backed structure typically requires D&O for board protection. No contract requirement, but standard for risk-tier matching Run-Test profile.
findings.policy_quote: No Directors & Officers policy in audit set.
findings.gap_description: PE-backed companies typically have D&O policies for: (1) board member personal indemnification, (2) entity coverage for securities-style claims (less common in private), (3) regulatory investigation coverage. Election services companies face heightened regulatory and political scrutiny — state secretaries of state, election integrity oversight, congressional inquiries, and potential litigation around election outcomes. Without D&O, individual directors and officers face personal exposure for any decisions challenged in litigation or investigation. PE sponsors typically require D&O as a baseline in portfolio companies; if not in place, the sponsor's expectations should be confirmed.
findings.plain_english: Election services puts directors and officers in the political crosshairs. Anytime an election outcome is challenged — whether legitimate or not — D&O is what protects board members and executives personally for the decisions they made. PE sponsors almost always require it for portfolio companies. We don't see D&O in the audit set. If it's not in place, every officer and director is personally exposed to any lawsuit or investigation about Run-Test's election services decisions.
findings.recommendation: Bind a D&O policy with $5M+ limit (consider $10M-$25M given regulatory/political profile), entity coverage Side A/B/C, regulatory investigation coverage including SOS and AG investigations, broad definition of 'Claim' to include written demands, and prior acts coverage extending back to the entity formation. Confirm bump-up exclusion is removed if PE sponsor anticipates exit. Travelers, Hartford, AIG, Beazley, Chubb appropriate markets. Consider Management Liability package combining D&O + EPLI + Crime + Fiduciary for cost efficiency.
discoveryQuestions: Does Run-Test's PE sponsor have an insurance covenant requiring D&O coverage at portfolio-company level, and what's the limit floor?
If a state secretary of state opened an investigation into a Run-Test election technology decision, who pays for the executives' personal legal defense?
Has the board or any officer ever been named in a complaint, demand letter, or subpoena related to election services? What happened?
Has your PE sponsor or transaction counsel reviewed the D&O coverage as part of the insurance covenant compliance?

findings.requirement_type: Property — Not in Audit Set
findings.contract_quote: Sacramento §IX (COC conditional) and general property exposure for elections-services manufacturer with high-value equipment.
findings.policy_quote: No Commercial Property policy in audit set.
findings.gap_description: Run-Test is a manufacturer with high-value equipment (printing, mailing, scanning, tabulation hardware), facility-based operations, and significant business interruption exposure tied to election cycles. A facility fire 30 days before a major election could be existential. Without a Property policy in audit set, building values, contents, business interruption limits, extra expense, dependent BI, and high-value-equipment scheduling cannot be verified.
findings.plain_english: You're a manufacturer with high-value equipment in a facility-based operation. A fire, flood, or major equipment failure 30 days before an election cycle could cripple the business — not just the property loss, but the lost revenue and the contractual breaches with counties whose ballots couldn't ship. We didn't see your Property policy. We need to confirm building values, contents limits, business interruption (with adequate indemnity period for election cycles — likely 18-24 months not the standard 12), and a sublimit-free schedule of high-value equipment.
findings.recommendation: Produce Commercial Property / Building & Contents policy. Verify (1) full replacement cost on building and contents, (2) high-value equipment scheduled at agreed value, (3) Business Interruption with 18-24 month indemnity period, (4) Extra Expense, (5) Contingent BI for key vendors and supply chain (paper, envelope, mail processing), (6) Equipment Breakdown coverage for printing/mailing equipment, (7) Ordinance & Law if applicable.

findings.requirement_type: Maricopa Claims-Made Retro Date — Cyber
findings.contract_quote: Maricopa §8.2.3: 'In the event that the insurance required is written on a claims-made basis, Contractor warrants that any retroactive date under the policy shall precede the effective date of this contract and either continuous coverage will be maintained, or an extended discovery period will be exercised for a period of two years beginning at the time work under this contract is completed.'
findings.policy_quote: No Cyber policy in audit set; retro date cannot be verified.
findings.gap_description: Maricopa requires that any claims-made policy (most prominently Cyber and any Professional Liability) have a retro date PRECEDING the contract effective date. Without seeing the Cyber policy (or its retro date), this cannot be confirmed. A retro date that post-dates the contract effective date would mean any pre-retro-date wrongful act is uninsured. For Cyber specifically, given Run-Test's data handling history (decades in elections), establishing a retro date that captures pre-bind exposure is important.
findings.plain_english: Cyber and E&O policies are 'claims-made' — the policy that pays is the one in force when the claim is made, not when the bad event happened. A 'retro date' tells the policy how far back it'll go to pick up old events. Maricopa requires that retro date to be BEFORE your contract with them started. If it isn't, anything that happened in the gap between retro date and contract date is uninsured. For Run-Test, with decades of voter data history, getting the right retro date is critical.
findings.recommendation: When Cyber and E&O policies are produced, verify retro dates precede each county contract effective date. If a gap exists, negotiate prior acts coverage extension with carrier (often available for nominal premium). Plan for 2-year ERP at any policy non-renewal/replacement event per Maricopa. Track all county contract effective dates centrally so retro is benchmarked at every renewal.
discoveryQuestions: What's the retro date on your current cyber policy, and how does it compare to when you started serving each county client?
Have you ever switched cyber carriers? If so, did the new carrier give you full prior acts, or did the retro date reset?
If a privacy incident from three years ago surfaced today, would the current cyber policy respond?
When the cyber policy renews next, who reviews the retro date specifically — and has anyone tied that review to county contract effective dates?

findings.requirement_type: Sacramento Claims-Made Retro Date & ERP — Professional
findings.contract_quote: Sacramento §V.A-C: 'The Retro Date must be shown, and must be on or before the date of the Agreement or the beginning of Agreement performance ... Insurance must be maintained and evidence of insurance must be provided for at least one (1) year after completion of the Agreement. ... If coverage is cancelled or non-renewed, and not replaced ... the CONTRACTOR must purchase extended reporting coverage for a minimum of one (1) year after completion of the Agreement.'
findings.policy_quote: No Professional Liability policy in audit set; retro date and ERP construction cannot be verified.
findings.gap_description: Sacramento independently mandates retro-on-or-before contract effective date AND a 1-year minimum ERP if claims-made coverage is cancelled/non-renewed. Without the Professional Liability policy, neither can be verified. For elections services, retro-date alignment to contract date is critical because the most likely E&O claim would relate to ballot accuracy or processing performed at the start of the engagement.
findings.plain_english: Sacramento has a stricter standard than Maricopa on this — retro date must be on or before the contract effective date, AND if you ever cancel/non-renew the E&O without replacing it with continuous-retro coverage, you must buy a 1-year tail (ERP) at minimum. We don't have the E&O to verify any of this. This is one of the highest-likelihood claim sources for an elections-services company; getting it wrong is genuinely existential.
findings.recommendation: When Professional Liability/E&O is produced: (1) verify retro date precedes each Sacramento (and Maricopa) contract effective date, (2) calendar a 1-year ERP purchase trigger at any cancellation/non-renewal, (3) maintain retro continuity through any carrier change. Best practice: secure ERP quote at policy bind so cost is locked. Consider 3-year ERP rather than 1-year for additional buffer.
discoveryQuestions: When you bound your professional liability policy, was the retro date set to capture all prior elections work, or just the carrier-specific bind date?
Has anyone confirmed the E&O retro date is on or before each county contract effective date — Sacramento, Maricopa, and the other 29 states?
If you decided to switch E&O carriers next year, do you have a process to either get full prior acts on the new policy or buy ERP on the old one?
What's the worst-case dollar value of an E&O claim you could face — say, a misprinted ballot batch in a major county? Have you sized the policy limit to that?
